analysis.one_liner: Restores pre-2017 corporate tax rates and closes a series of loopholes that let multinational corporations avoid US taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from April 2024 until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the top corporate tax rate from 21% back to 35% and restore a tiered rate structure, including a 34% rate for income between $75,000 and $10 million. It would also tax the foreign profits of US-owned subsidiaries the same as domestic profits, end rules that let companies reclassify foreign entities to avoid taxes, tighten rules against corporate inversions (moving headquarters abroad on paper), limit deductible interest for members of multinational groups, crack down on treaty shopping, and repeal the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income. Together, these changes are designed to stop multinational corporations from shifting profits offshore to lower their US tax bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers as a group, who would bear a smaller share of federal revenue needs if corporations paid taxes on profits they currently shift offshore. Domestic-only companies that already pay the full US rate would also compete on more even footing against multinationals that use offshore structures.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would restore a graduated corporate rate structure topping out at 35%, up from the flat 21% rate set by the 2017 tax law, and apply it to years beginning after December 31, 2024 [S2].
It would treat all income of controlled foreign corporations (US-owned foreign subsidiaries) as taxable subpart F income, ending the preference for foreign profits under current law [S2].
It would repeal the check-the-box rules for certain foreign entities and the look-through rule for related-party payments, two widely used vehicles for shifting income to low-tax countries [S2].
It would tighten anti-inversion rules, treating foreign companies that are actually managed and controlled in the United States as domestic corporations subject to US tax [S2].
It would raise and strengthen the base erosion and anti-abuse tax (BEAT), which targets companies that strip profits out of the US through payments to foreign affiliates [S2].

It would deny foreign tax credits for levies paid by oil, gas, and mining companies that receive special economic benefits from foreign governments, and would repeal the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income, a provision that lowered the effective rate on profits attributed to foreign markets [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations and their shareholders, who would face a higher top rate (35% versus 21%), taxation of foreign subsidiary income, loss of the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and new limits on interest deductions and treaty benefits.

drawbacks.text: Raising the top corporate rate from 21% to 35% would reverse a central feature of the 2017 tax law; critics argue a 35% rate puts US-based multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors taxed at lower home-country rates [S2].

The bill would override US treaty obligations for some provisions, applying its rules "without regard to any treaty obligation of the United States" — a step that trading partners and treaty negotiators generally oppose because it disrupts agreed international tax rules [S2].

Fully taxing all foreign subsidiary income each year, with accelerated collection of previously deferred amounts, would be a major shift in how US companies with overseas operations are taxed and could discourage American companies from expanding abroad [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would substantially increase what multinationals pay in US taxes, which would reduce pressure on other taxpayers and even the field for domestic-only firms. The costs are real: a 35% top rate and full taxation of foreign income would likely reduce some US corporate investment abroad and raise compliance complexity, and overriding tax treaties could create friction with trading partners. On balance, the bill is a straightforward transfer of tax burden from everyday taxpayers toward large multinationals, with the strongest honest objection being its aggressive reversal of the 2017 international tax framework.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act in the House on April 10, 2024 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day it was introduced; that referral is the only action recorded in its history [S4].
The bill had two cosponsors, both Democrats, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the committee or the House ever taking it up [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and their shareholders are better off: the lower 21% corporate rate, the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and the offshore profit-shifting tools the bill targeted all remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on April 10, 2024.

for.name: Two Democratic House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it had no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 10, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote; the referral is the last recorded action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-controlled House never gave the bill any committee or floor action [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill targets the core tools multinationals use to shift profits offshore and pay lower US rates: it would tax foreign subsidiary income, end check-the-box planning, tighten anti-inversion rules, and restore the 35% top rate. Their gain in keeping the status quo is the ordinary taxpayer's cost of covering the revenue gap [S2].

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mining companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The bill would deny foreign tax credits for foreign levies where the company receives a special economic benefit from the foreign government, closing a credit that reduces these companies' US tax bills. Companies that rely on this credit would bear more tax; the general taxpayer gains the revenue [S2].

industries.industry: US companies earning foreign-derived intangible income (notably pharmaceutical and technology firms)
industries.note: The bill would repeal the FDII deduction, which lowers the effective tax rate on profits attributed to serving foreign markets from the US. Repeal raises taxes on these firms but removes a break that primarily benefits large profitable multinationals [S2].

industries.industry: Corporate tax planning structures and treaty-shopping arrangements
industries.note: New limits on treaty benefits for related-party payments and for income routed through low-tax third countries would shut down conduit arrangements used to avoid US withholding tax [S2].
